claims.claim: Both own the clock, so no caller derives a timestamp with `date` and no caller invents a second duration format.
claims.what_the_code_does: False phrases: "Both own the clock" and "no caller derives a timestamp with `date`". Only `run-timed-command` owns both ends of its interval. `record-timing-event` always stamps the END itself, but its START comes from the caller whenever `--started-at <RFC3339>` is passed, and the shipped caller passes one: actions/work.md Step 5 tells the owner to hold the current UTC instant and then record the delegated wait with `--category builder-work --started-at <the instant you held>`. The instant is obtained through the Timestamp rule, whose option 1 is `do-work-cli.sh --format text now` but whose option 2 is literally `date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ`, so on the POSIX floor a caller does derive a timestamp with `date`. Without `--started-at`, record-timing-event chains the start to the previous event's end (or to its own end on an empty stream). The duration half is true and stronger than stated: no verb accepts a duration at all, so a caller cannot supply one.
claims.evidence: internal/lifecycletiming/timing_commands.go:188-193 parses `--started-at` into options.startedAt/hasStartedAt; internal/lifecycletiming/lifecycle_timing.go:135 AppendTimingEvent stamps endInstant itself, :281 falls back to defaultStartInstant only when HasExplicitStart is false, :322 defaultStartInstant chains to the previous event's end; :170-172 RunTimedCommand reads both ends with timingClockNow(). Caller: skills/do-work/actions/work.md:284; floor command: skills/do-work/actions/work-reference.md Timestamp rule option 2. Measured on the built binary: `record-timing-event ... --elapsed 5` -> `finding TIMING-USAGE [error]: unknown option "--elapsed"`; two chained events with no `--started-at` produced started_at equal to the prior ended_at.
claims.suggested_text: Both stamp the event's end themselves and derive its elapsed seconds themselves, and neither accepts a duration, so no caller invents a second duration format. `run-timed-command` owns both ends outright. `record-timing-event` owns the start too when none is given, chaining the event to the previous event's end (or to its own end on an empty stream); a caller pins `--started-at <RFC3339>` only when it already held the start of a delegated interval, and it obtains that instant through the Timestamp rule (`actions/work-reference.md`), never from a format of its own.

claims.claim: The wrapper attaches the child's own stdout and stderr to the console rather than a pipe, and exits with the child's status: the child's own code, 128 plus the signal number when a signal killed it, and 127 when the command never launched.
claims.what_the_code_does: False phrase: "the child's own stdout and stderr to the console". The wrapper points BOTH child streams at one writer, and main passes os.Stderr for it, so the child's stdout is merged onto the CLI's stderr rather than staying on stdout. That is deliberate: it keeps the CLI's stdout free for the rendered CommandResult. The consequence the current wording hides is that a caller who redirects the CLI's stdout to capture the wrapped gate's output captures the rendered result instead and gets none of the child's bytes. "Rather than a pipe" is correct (os.Stderr is a real file descriptor, passed straight to the child). The exit-status clause is fully accurate.
claims.evidence: internal/lifecycletiming/lifecycle_timing.go:167-168 `command.Stdout = childOutput` and `command.Stderr = childOutput`; internal/lifecycletiming/timing_commands.go:21-23 comment "childOutput receives a wrapped command's own stdout and stderr, which keeps stdout free for the rendered CommandResult; main passes os.Stderr"; cmd/do-work-cli/main.go:47 `lifecycletiming.Handlers(os.Stderr)` versus :80 `commandruntime.NewRuntime(os.Stdout, handlers)`. Measured on the built binary with `-- sh -c 'echo CHILD_STDOUT; echo CHILD_STDERR >&2; exit 3'`: the stdout redirect file held only the rendered result, the stderr redirect file held both CHILD_STDOUT and CHILD_STDERR, and the process exited 3. `kill -TERM $$` exited 143; a nonexistent binary exited 127.
claims.suggested_text: The wrapper hands the child the CLI's own stderr handle for both its stdout and its stderr — a file descriptor, not a pipe — which keeps the CLI's stdout free for the rendered result: redirect stdout and you capture the result, never the wrapped command's output. It exits with the child's status: the child's own code, 128 plus the signal number when a signal killed it, and 127 when the command never launched.

claims.claim: Timing evidence is metadata only. A command reaches the stream as its executable's base name plus an argv token count, never as arguments, so a token or a user-controlled path cannot land in durable evidence.
claims.what_the_code_does: False phrase: "so a token or a user-controlled path cannot land in durable evidence" (and the umbrella "Timing evidence is metadata only" that sets it up). The redaction is real but covers exactly one field. `--operation` is free caller text: it reaches the stream as written and RenderTimingSection prints it verbatim into the folded `## Timing` section, which is what remains in the request file after the fold deletes the stream. `--agent` and `--revision` are free text too and reach the stream, but not the folded section. The only processing on any of them is boundEvidenceText: control characters and `|` removed, whitespace collapsed, cut to 120 runes. That is bounding, not redaction.
claims.evidence: internal/lifecycletiming/lifecycle_timing.go:702-712 redactCommandIdentity emits `<base name> (N argv tokens)`; :307 CommandIdentity is the only redacted field while Operation/Revision/ResponsibleAgent pass through boundEvidenceText; :716-731 boundEvidenceText with evidenceTextLimit = 120 at :104; :483-506 RenderTimingSection prints Category, Operation, elapsed, Outcome, ExitStatus and CommandIdentity only. Measured on the built binary: `record-timing-event --operation "fetch /home/alice/.ssh/id_rsa with token ghp_ABC123SECRET" --agent alice@example.com --revision abc123 --command "curl -H Authorization: Bearer ghp_ABC123SECRET https://x"` wrote command_identity `"curl (6 argv tokens)"` but operation in full; the subsequent fold wrote `Slowest command: builder-work / fetch /home/alice/.ssh/id_rsa with token ghp_ABC123SECRET, ...` into the request file, with no agent and no revision.
claims.suggested_text: A command reaches the stream as its executable's base name plus an argv token count, never as arguments, so no argument value can land in durable evidence. That redaction covers the command and nothing else. `--operation` is free caller text: it reaches the stream and is printed into the folded `## Timing` section, which is what survives in the request file after the stream is deleted — so never build one out of a token, a secret, or a user-controlled path. `--agent` and `--revision` are free text too and reach the stream, though not the folded section. All three are only stripped of control characters and `|`, collapsed to one line, and cut to 120 characters; none of that is redaction.

The Go handler resolves the argument with `git rev-parse --verify <commit>^{commit}`, then builds `<revision>^2` as an argv element and runs `git rev-parse --verify -q` on it through exec.Command with no shell in between; the retained launcher only rewrites a single positional into `--commit` before exec'ing the CLI. claims.claim: `git show --name-only --format=` is acceptable when a caller genuinely needs show
claims.what_the_code_does: False phrase: "is acceptable when a caller genuinely needs show", stated without the parent-count condition. It is fine on a single-parent commit and silently empty on a merge — exactly the trap the Merge-aware commit diff section twelve lines above exists to warn about. A path-only consumer reads that empty output as a commit that touched no files.
claims.evidence: Measured, git 2.43.0, scratch repo with a real two-parent merge: `git show --name-only --format= HEAD` produced no output and exited 0, while the same commit's paths are `side.txt` and `main.txt` (`git show --name-only --format= -m HEAD` and `git diff-tree --no-commit-id --name-only -r -m HEAD` both list them). On the ordinary commit `HEAD~1` the same command printed `main.txt`.
claims.suggested_text: `git show --name-only --format=` is acceptable only for a commit already known to have one parent. On a merge it prints nothing at all, which a path-only consumer reads as a commit that changed no files — the same silent empty the section above exists to prevent.

claims.claim: the diff-tree form above is the suite default for path-only consumers.
claims.what_the_code_does: False phrase: "is the suite default for path-only consumers". Nothing in the suite runs the printed form. No shipped action file and no shipped script contains `diff-tree` at all — the only occurrence under skills/ is this guide line itself. The three path-only diff-tree call sites are all in Go and all carry different flags, and none of them matches the printed form: gate evidence adds `-z`, the Git transaction drops `-m` and adds `--root -z`, and finalization drops `-m` and `-z` both. So the form is a recommendation with no consumer, described as a default.
claims.evidence: internal/gateevidence/gate_evidence.go:377 `diff-tree --no-commit-id --name-only -r -m -z <commit>` inside interveningCommitsAreGateLogs, which walks every commit in `recorded..HEAD`; internal/gittransaction/git_transaction.go:1375 `diff-tree --root --no-commit-id --name-only -r -z <commitSHA>` in committedPaths, called at :659 on the SHA read from HEAD immediately after the transaction's own commit; internal/finalization/finalization_apply.go:545 `diff-tree --no-commit-id --name-only -r <candidate>` in matchingHeadCommit, after a `git diff --binary` digest match. `grep -rn "diff-tree" skills/ --include=*.md --include=*.sh` returns only prescribed-shell-primitives.md:90 and :93. Measured: `-m` emits one row per parent, so a file changed on both sides of a merge (`shared.txt`) is listed twice.
claims.suggested_text: Take the rest of the flags from the input rather than copying one house form. `-m` is what makes the listing non-empty on a merge, and it emits one row per parent, so a path changed on both sides appears twice; `-z` is what keeps a filename carrying a space, quote, or newline readable. The shipped Go consumers each carry what their own input needs: gate evidence walks arbitrary commits and carries `-m -z`, the Git transaction reads back the single-parent commit it just made and carries `--root -z`, and finalization matches candidate commits against a recorded diff digest and carries neither.

claims.claim: Whenever a publication's destination could already be occupied, the publishing step verifies the path it actually wrote; the rename's or link's exit status is not that proof.
claims.what_the_code_does: False phrase: "the publishing step verifies the path it actually wrote", stated flatly and extended at line 109 to "every publication described below". Exactly one shipped publication does that. capture-screenshot links its stage into place and then stats both names and compares them with os.SameFile. atomic-download stats the target only to read a byte count and discards the error. The portfolio helper's rootedPublishFile does no post-publication identity check at all. The section also already contradicts itself: line 125 says of the two publications that "only one of them verifies". The second clause is right about shell and wrong about the helpers: for them the call's own error IS the answer, but only within its limits — `link` refuses every existing destination, while `rename` refuses only a directory and silently replaces an occupying regular file.
claims.evidence: Verifies: internal/corehelpers/publication.go:178 `parentRoot.Link(temporaryName, destinationName)` then :180-183 Stat both names and `os.SameFile`. Does not: internal/corehelpers/commands.go:888 `os.Rename(temporaryPath, targetPath)` then :891 `info, _ := os.Stat(targetPath)` for the size only; internal/toolboxcommands/mutation.go:190 `parent.Rename` / :196 `parent.Link` with no check after either. Syscall limits measured on this filesystem: `link(2)` file over an existing directory -> EEXIST (17); `rename(2)` file over an empty AND over a non-empty directory -> EISDIR (21); `rename(2)` over an existing regular file succeeds and replaces it, which is why atomic-download needs its own directory pre-check at commands.go:869-871 and rootedPublishFile needs its own regular-file pre-check at mutation.go:148-151.

The others take the proof from the call itself — which is sound only as far as the call goes, because `link` refuses every existing destination while `rename` refuses only a directory and silently replaces an occupying file. A step that must not replace a file says so in its own section.

claims.claim: `ln` and `mv` treat a directory standing in the destination's place as a container rather than a collision, so the payload lands inside it under the private staging name, the command exits zero, and the destination is still the directory it was.
claims.what_the_code_does: The sentence is true of `ln` and `mv` and false as a description of anything the suite runs, and it is the half of the guide that leaves the reader unable to reconcile line 125's "a rename over one fails". No shipped publication uses shell `ln` or `mv`: every one publishes through Go's link and rename, which refuse an occupying directory outright. The only shell `mv` left anywhere under skills/ is in the installer's bootstrap heredoc, moving a download into a fresh mktemp directory, which is not a publication. The fix is not to delete the sentence — the shell behavior is real and still governs hand-written blocks — but to say which behavior belongs to which, so both sections read as one statement.
claims.evidence: Shipped publication calls: internal/corehelpers/publication.go:178 `parentRoot.Link`; internal/corehelpers/commands.go:888 `os.Rename`; internal/toolboxcommands/mutation.go:190 `parent.Rename` and :196 `parent.Link`, :270 `directory.Link`; internal/atomicfile/atomic_replace_unix.go:8 `os.Rename`; internal/archivefetch/archive_fetch.go:177/370/379. `grep -rnw 'ln' skills/` and `grep -rn '\bmv\b' skills/` find no publication use; the sole shell `mv` is skills/do-work/tools/install-do-work-suite.sh:25 inside the `--print-bootstrap-command` heredoc. Measured on this filesystem: shell `mv .occupied.publishing.abc occupied` and `ln .occupied.publishing.abc occupied` against a directory named `occupied` each exited 0 and left the staging file inside it; `link(2)` returned EEXIST and `rename(2)` returned EISDIR against the same destination and wrote nothing; Go's `os.Rename`, `os.Link` and `Root.Link` all returned "file exists" and `Root.Rename` returned "is a directory", leaving the destination directory empty.
claims.suggested_text: The shell utilities and the syscalls disagree here, and that disagreement is the whole reason the check exists. `ln` and `mv` treat a directory standing in the destination's place as a container rather than a collision: the payload lands inside it under the private staging name, the command exits zero, and the destination is still the directory it was. `link(2)` and `rename(2)` — what the shipped publications actually call — refuse that destination with `EEXIST` and `EISDIR` and write nothing. So hand-written shell has to make the check for itself, while a Go helper can read it off the error it already has.

claims.claim: The canonical command copies and verifies that source into a private file adjacent to the canonical target, once per output.
claims.what_the_code_does: Three of the four clauses are wrong. "copies ... that source ... once per output": the source is read once into memory and both outputs are written from that one buffer, so there is no per-output copy of the source. "verifies": nothing reads the staged bytes back — the stage is written, synced and closed, and that is all. The only checks are that the source is a regular file, and, on a replace, that the existing canonical file is still the same inode with the same bytes it was read as. "adjacent to the canonical target": the stage is created beside the output being published, so with `--with-snapshot` the snapshot's stage lands in the snapshot directory, a different directory from the canonical file's. "once per output" is true only of the staging file itself.

Different directories in the shipped caller: skills/do-work-toolbox/actions/present-work.md:133-134 — canonical `do-work/deliverables/portfolio-summary.md`, snapshot under `do-work/deliverables/portfolio-snapshots/`.
claims.suggested_text: The canonical command reads that source once, confirms it is a regular file, and publishes every output from those same bytes. Each output is staged in a private dot-file beside its own destination — the snapshot in the snapshot directory, the canonical file in the canonical one — written, synced, then linked or renamed into place. Nothing reads the staged bytes back; the check the command does make before replacing an existing canonical file is that the file it is about to replace is still, inode and bytes, the regular file it read a moment earlier.

sweep_suggestions_that_were_wrong:
Four of the sweep's ten suggestions would have put a NEW false sentence into the guide. Listed worst first.

W1 — claim at line 107, the `ln`/`mv` sentence. The sweep's suggested_text opens "Go's `os.Rename` and `os.Link` refuse a destination that already exists". That is false for `os.Rename`: rename(2) replaces an existing regular file silently and refuses only a directory. I measured it — rename over a regular file succeeds. The sweep's own evidence line shows why it slipped: it tested only a directory destination ("Go -> rename ...: file exists") and compressed that single measurement into a general claim about any existing destination. This is the same compression failure the request describes. It also matters downstream: atomic-download would silently overwrite an occupying file, and the guide would be telling the reader the syscall prevents that.

W2 — claim at line 107, first sentence. The sweep's suggested_text says "`atomic-download` and `publish-portfolio-summary` take the proof from the syscall instead, which refuses an occupied destination rather than writing under it." Wrong for atomic-download for the reason in W1: its protection against a directory is an explicit `os.Lstat`/`IsDir` pre-check at internal/corehelpers/commands.go:869-871, not the rename, and it has no protection against an occupying regular file at all. Its what_the_code_does is also unfair to the portfolio helper — "takes the Link's or Rename's return value as the whole answer with no post-publication identity check" is right about the post-publication half but omits the pre-replace check at internal/toolboxcommands/mutation.go:148-151 and :186-188, which requires the target to be a regular file and to be byte-identical to what was read.

W3 — claim at line 32. The sweep's suggested_text says the `--operation`, `--agent` and `--revision` labels "travel as written into both the stream and the folded `## Timing` section". `--agent` and `--revision` reach the stream only. RenderTimingSection (internal/lifecycletiming/lifecycle_timing.go:483-506) prints Category, Operation, elapsed, Outcome, ExitStatus and CommandIdentity and nothing else. I folded a real event carrying `--agent alice@example.com --revision abc123` and neither appeared in the section.

W4 — claim at line 30, the clock sentence. The sweep's suggested_text says record-timing-event "takes an explicit `--started-at` only for a delegated interval whose start the caller already held". The "only" is not in the code: `--started-at` is accepted on any record-timing-event invocation, in any category, with no gate (internal/lifecycletiming/timing_commands.go:188-193). It describes the shipped convention in actions/work.md, not a constraint the command enforces, and stating it as a rule would be a fresh false claim of the same kind.

Not wrong, but incomplete: the claim at line 93 ("suite default"). The sweep's suggested_text names gateevidence and gittransaction but silently drops finalization, which its own what_the_code_does had identified as the third consumer and the one that carries neither flag. Dropping the one consumer whose flag set is most surprising weakens the point the sentence is making.
notes:
Method: every claim was re-derived from the Go source, and every filesystem or Git behavior in it was measured rather than reasoned about. I built the CLI (go1.26.1, `go build ./cmd/do-work-cli`, exit 0) and ran record-timing-event, run-timed-command, fold-timing-summary and show-commit-diff against scratch repositories; I ran shell `mv`/`ln`, `rename(2)`/`link(2)` via Python, and Go's os.Rename/os.Link/Root.Link/Root.Rename against a directory destination; and I built a real two-parent merge to test `git show --name-only --format=` and the diff-tree forms.

Three things sit just outside my ten claims but will break the sections I am correcting if they are left alone.

N1 — line 129, the sentence between claim 28 and claim 30, which the sweep marked accurate: "`--with-snapshot` first publishes an exclusive snapshot from its own verified copy". "Verified copy" is the same word claim 28 makes false. There is no verified copy — the stage is written from the in-memory buffer and never read back (internal/toolboxcommands/mutation.go:171-179). Fixing claim 28 and leaving this makes the paragraph contradict itself in two adjacent sentences. The same false claim is repeated in the consuming action at skills/do-work-toolbox/actions/present-work.md:137, "the helper verifies each output against the source separately".

N2 — the nonexistent-script problem is not confined to claim 30. skills/do-work-toolbox/actions/present-work.md:141 says "do not fall back to the compatibility script", naming the same script that does not exist. And the Report image batch section at guide line 137 says "rather than orchestrating the retained scripts yourself" and "a retained script is not a fallback" — `find skills -iname '*report-image*'` returns no script either, only internal/toolboxcommands/report_image.go. Whoever fixes claim 30 should sweep the condition rather than the one sentence, or the same defect stays in two more places.

N3 — atomic-download is asymmetric in a way the guide never mentions: its `--dry-run` path refuses ANY existing target (internal/corehelpers/commands.go:863-865, DOWNLOAD-TARGET-OCCUPIED "target already exists"), while the real run refuses only a directory (:869-871, "target is a directory") and then lets os.Rename replace an occupying regular file. A reader who validates with --dry-run and then runs for real gets two different occupancy policies.

One latent hazard found while deriving claim 18, reported because it is the exact trap the guide's own Merge-aware section names, not because it is a guide claim: internal/finalization/finalization_apply.go:545 runs diff-tree without `-m`, so a merge among the candidates in `PreparedHead..HEAD` lists no paths, and the `exact` loop over an empty list stays true. The preceding `git diff --binary` digest match at :541-543 is what keeps this from being reachable today. Worth a REQ, not a guide edit.

claims.claim: "Both own the clock, so no caller derives a timestamp with `date` and no caller invents a second duration format."
claims.what_the_code_does: Only run-timed-command owns both ends of the clock (lifecycle_timing.go:170-172, elapsed reported as monotonic_in_process at :193-198). record-timing-event owns the END instant only (lifecycle_timing.go:135); the START is either chained to the previous event's end (defaultStartInstant, lifecycle_timing.go:280-282, 322-329) or supplied by the caller as `--started-at <RFC3339>` (timing_commands.go:188-193). The duration half of the sentence is true of both verbs: elapsed is derived in Go and rendered by formatElapsedSeconds (lifecycle_timing.go:740-755).

claims.claim: "The wrapper attaches the child's own stdout and stderr to the console rather than a pipe"
claims.what_the_code_does: Both child streams are set to one writer (lifecycle_timing.go:167-168 `command.Stdout = childOutput`, `command.Stderr = childOutput`), and main passes os.Stderr for it (cmd/do-work-cli/main.go:47 `lifecycletiming.Handlers(os.Stderr)`). So the child's stdout is merged onto the CLI's stderr, deliberately, to keep the CLI's stdout free for the rendered CommandResult (timing_commands.go:21-23). git diff-tree --no-commit-id --name-only -r -m <commit>

sweep_suggestions_that_were_wrong:
Four of the prior sweep's drafts would have shipped a new false sentence, which is why I re-derived every one.

1. Line 106/107, the biggest one. The sweep's replacement says "Go's `os.Rename` and `os.Link` refuse a destination that already exists", and its other draft says atomic-download and publish-portfolio-summary "take the proof from the syscall instead, which refuses an occupied destination rather than writing under it". os.Rename refuses only a *directory* destination. I measured it: renaming a staging file onto an existing regular file returned nil and replaced the file's contents. atomic-download depends on exactly that (internal/corehelpers/commands.go:888 replaces an occupied regular target silently; only a directory is refused at :869), and the portfolio replace path is also a rename over an existing file (internal/toolboxcommands/mutation.go:190). Publishing the sweep's sentence would have put a false absolute into the section whose whole subject is what a syscall does and does not guarantee.

2. Line 32, timing evidence. The sweep says the caller-written `--operation`, `--agent` and `--revision` labels "travel as written into both the stream and the folded `## Timing` section". Only `--operation` reaches the section, and only for the slowest stage and slowest command rows: RenderTimingSection prints category, operation, elapsed, outcome, exit status and the redacted command identity and nothing else (internal/lifecycletiming/lifecycle_timing.go:483-509). `--agent` and `--revision` stay in the Git-private stream, which the fold then deletes. My fixture with all three set confirmed it — the agent and revision text appeared in the .jsonl and never in the request file.

3. Line 92, the show form. The sweep says that on a two-parent merge "without `-m` it prints nothing at all there". That holds only for a conflict-free merge. On a merge that had a conflict, `git show --name-only --format=` printed the conflict-resolved path and nothing else — a plausible, short, wrong answer, which is more dangerous than empty output and is the case the replacement text should name.

4. Line 92, the diff-tree flags. The sweep's replacement says `-z` "is what makes it safe for a filename carrying a space, quote or newline".
